items.title: Characterizing Memory Misalignment in Human-LLM Interaction From User Perspectives
items.abstract: While memory enhances personalization in LLM-based conversational agents, it suffers from memory misalignment, where memories violate user expectations. We present a mixed-methods investigation to characterize and mitigate memory misalignment from user perspectives. First, we collected data from memory usage (N=28, 457 entries) and diary study (N=32, 304 reports), which yielded a taxonomy spanning 14 misalignment types across memory intake, storage and management, retrieval and interpretation stages. Second, four co-design workshops with 12 experienced HCI researchers derived a design space to tackle memory misalignment issues, consisting of 12 candidate interaction strategies structured across interaction form, placement and intrusiveness dimensions. Finally, a speed dating with 121 users reveals preference heterogeneity, where users prioritize proactive controls over cognitively demanding causal graph inspections or passive audit logs. Synthesizing these findings, we highlight the tension between supervisory agency and interaction overhead, and advocate for friction-aware memories that balance user oversight with conversation smoothness.

items.title: ChatGPT-Assisted Learning Effectiveness and Students’ Academic Outcomes: A Mediation Analysis of Cognitive Engagement and Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the association between ChatGPT-assisted learning effectiveness and students’ academic performance, emphasizing the mediating roles of cognitive engagement and academic self-efficacy. Data were collected from tourism and hospitality students at Egyptian universities. Findings indicate that perceived ChatGPT-assisted learning effectiveness is positively associated with students’ academic performance, cognitive engagement, and academic self-efficacy. Cognitive engagement and academic self-efficacy also show significant positive associations with academic performance, and both constructs significantly mediate the relationship between ChatGPT-assisted learning effectiveness and academic performance. These findings suggest that the educational value students attribute to ChatGPT may operate through complementary cognitive and motivational pathways, while the cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions.

items.title: Convenience Amid Crisis: Explaining Generative AI Misuse and Compliance Intention Among Myanmar University Students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education, creating opportunities for learning alongside concerns about academic integrity and institutional governance. This study used the Theory of Planned Behavior to examine behavioral, institutional, and psychological factors linked to self-reported AI Misuse and Compliance Intention among students at Myanmar universities, a higher education system that has faced substantial upheaval since 2021. A cross-sectional, seven-point Likert-scale survey (twelve constructs) was administered to 851 students across six institutions, capturing constructs such as Rule Clarity, Institutional Enforcement, Behavioral Control, and Academic Pressure. An exploratory factor analysis confirmed the twelve constructs were empirically distinct. Two multiple linear regression models produced distinct predictor patterns for each outcome. AI Misuse rose most with Misuse Acceptability and Moral Rationalization, and fell most with Institutional Enforcement. Compliance Intention rose most with Behavioral Control, Institutional Enforcement, and Subjective Norms, and fell with Academic Pressure. AI Familiarity did not significantly predict either outcome, and Subjective Norms did not predict AI Misuse. Academic Pressure played a dual role, raising AI Misuse while lowering Compliance Intention — evidence that situational strain can push students toward rule-breaking while eroding their commitment to institutional expectations. Overall, students’ choices around AI appeared driven less by exposure to the technology itself and more by their attitudes, ethical reasoning, and views of institutional governance. These results point toward institutional strategies that pair clear policy with authentic assessment design and efforts to build students’ independent academic judgment and manage Academic Pressure.

items.title: Criminal responsibility in black-box AI crime: Re-interpretation of foreseeability and inspirations for Canadian AI regulations
items.abstract: Perpetrators using artificial intelligence (AI) to commit crime challenge the traditional criminal liability framework centred on foreseeability. This article argues that such a challenge is particularly acute in AI systems with black-box algorithms: perpetrators may exploit the lack of algorithmic transparency to claim they could not anticipate AI's output, thereby avoiding liability for criminal consequences, exceeding their mens rea . To circumvent the issue, this article adopts a novel knowledge-based approach to reinterpret the notion of foreseeability, and distinguishes between strict and relaxed interpretations of foreseeability, depending on the perpetrator's expected knowledge of criminal consequences. The strict interpretation is evident in the traditional doctrine, which requires knowledge only when perpetrators are expected to manipulate the criminal consequences. The relaxed interpretation suffices if the perpetrator knows the black-box AI will execute its programmed instructions without refusal, thus preventing them from evading responsibility by appealing to algorithmic opacity. The justification for the knowledge-based interpretation derives from preserving the autonomy of humans. This article further argues that AI systems should be designed to prevent and refuse participation in actus reus and should be subject to technical regulation. It also puts forward nuanced recommendations for Canada to enhance AI governance and anti-fraud regulation.

items.title: Democratic Algorithmic Accountability Framework (DAAF): A Methodological and Engineering Model for Algorithmic Governance and AI Act Compliance in the Social Economy
items.abstract: Executive Summary Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act ("AI Act"), together with the GDPR and the Data Governance Act, imposes upon organisations a structural redesign of the management of algorithmic systems, particularly where such systems are deployed in workforce management and in high-impact decision-making processes. For the cooperative and social economy, this transition is not merely a matter of regulatory compliance. It constitutes a challenge bearing upon the very identity of the organisation: preserving the foundational democratic principle, "one member, one vote", and the centrality of the human person in the face of the opacity of machine learning models. The scholarly literature and the frameworks available on the market reveal an evident methodological gap. On the one hand, there exist rather abstract technical-organisational compliance standards, such as ISO/IEC 42001, or ethical mapping exercises devoid of genuine operational traction. On the other hand, integrated models capable of translating the legal requirements of human oversight into engineering workflows consistent with mutualistic principles are lacking. The Democratic Algorithmic Accountability Framework (DAAF) has been developed to bridge this divide by integrating three disciplines: public and administrative law, through the extension of the meta-principle of algorithmic legality; management engineering, through Business Process Reengineering and the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle; and data governance, through immutable audit registers and explainability protocols designated as TRACE. The framework has been empirically validated through the operational platform AGORA, whose recommendation engine has accumulated over 56,000 immutable audit logs across a 19-month horizon.

items.title: Developing and Validating an AI Literacy Instrument for Elementary School Students: A Psychometric Study Using the ADDIE Framework
items.abstract: AbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) literacy has emerged as a critical competency in elementary education as learners increasingly engage with AI-mediated and technology-rich learning environments. This study developed and validated a multidimensional AI literacy instrument for elementary school students using a research and development approach grounded in the ADDIE framework and informed by AI literacy, constructivist learning, and digital citizenship theories. The instrument comprised five dimensions: AI recognition, conceptual understanding, functional application, evaluation and creation, and AI ethics. Content validation by four experts demonstrated strong theoretical relevance across all dimensions. Empirical testing involving 250 Indonesian elementary school students examined the instrument’s psychometric properties. Exploratory factor analysis supported a five-factor structure with acceptable factor loadings and sampling adequacy (KMO > .80; Bartlett’s test, p < .001), explaining a substantial proportion of total variance. Reliability analysis indicated satisfactory internal consistency across retained subscales (Cronbach’s α > .70), although conceptual understanding required minor item revision. Descriptive findings revealed stronger competencies in ethical AI use and functional application than in conceptual understanding of AI processes. The study contributes a psychometrically grounded and developmentally appropriate instrument supporting AI literacy assessment, curriculum innovation, instructional evaluation, and responsible AI integration within primary education contexts for early twenty-first-century educational transformation. Bendo is an active researcher and academic writer pursuing a Bachelor of Science in Entrepreneurship at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines–Maragondon Campus. His research focuses on digital and mobile learning environments, artificial intelligence in education, educational psychology, educational assessment, psychometrics, and financial technology (FinTech), with emphasis on technology-mediated learning, learner engagement, digital participation, and emerging educational innovations. He has authored several studies published and forthcoming in international and Scopus-indexed journals. items.title: Developing and Validating an AI Literacy Instrument for Elementary School Students: A Psychometric Study Using the ADDIE Framework
items.abstract: AbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) literacy has emerged as a critical competency in elementary education as learners increasingly engage with AI-mediated and technology-rich learning environments. This study developed and validated a multidimensional AI literacy instrument for elementary school students using a research and development approach grounded in the ADDIE framework and informed by AI literacy, constructivist learning, and digital citizenship theories. The instrument comprised five dimensions: AI recognition, conceptual understanding, functional application, evaluation and creation, and AI ethics. Content validation by four experts demonstrated strong theoretical relevance across all dimensions. Empirical testing involving 250 Indonesian elementary school students examined the instrument’s psychometric properties. Exploratory factor analysis supported a five-factor structure with acceptable factor loadings and sampling adequacy (KMO > .80; Bartlett’s test, p < .001), explaining a substantial proportion of total variance. Reliability analysis indicated satisfactory internal consistency across retained subscales (Cronbach’s α > .70), although conceptual understanding required minor item revision. Descriptive findings revealed stronger competencies in ethical AI use and functional application than in conceptual understanding of AI processes. The study contributes a psychometrically grounded and developmentally appropriate instrument supporting AI literacy assessment, curriculum innovation, instructional evaluation, and responsible AI integration within primary education contexts for early twenty-first-century educational transformation. items.title: Distinguishing AI-generated and real images: implications for media literacy instruction
items.abstract: This study aimed to assess the detection accuracy and usefulness of determinants for distinguishing artificial intelligence (AI)-generated and real images among senior high school students in Western Visayas during the academic year 2025–2026. It examined the significant differences in the two mentioned constructs across students’ demographic profiles. It employed a quantitative design- the descriptive-comparative approach. A random sample of 104 students was involved, using a validated, reliability-tested 33-item researcher-made questionnaire. Descriptive and comparative statistical analyses were employed. Mean, standard deviation (SD), Mann-Whitney U test, and Kruskal-Wallis H test were used. The findings revealed that the students demonstrated a moderate level of detection accuracy (M=5.16, SD=1.61). The students rated the usefulness of the determinants as helpful (M=3.78, SD=0.74). Additionally, it was found that there is a significant difference in detection accuracy when grouped by school type [U=965.500, p=0.011] compared to its counterparts. Significant differences were found in the usefulness of determinants for distinguishing AI from real images when grouped by type of school [U=815.000, p=0.001] and frequency of use of AI [H(2)=11.989, p=0.002]. The findings of the study may provide teachers with insights into developing instructional strategies and interventions to enhance students’ critical thinking and digital literacy skills.

items.title: Effectiveness of artificial intelligence augmented teachers’ autonomy support instructional strategy on students’ achievement in mathematics-related biology topics
items.abstract: The study examined the effectiveness of “artificial intelligence augmented teachers’ autonomy support” (AIATAS) instructional strategy on students’ achievement in mathematics-related biology topics. The study adopted a pre-/post-test, non-equivalent control group quasi-experimental design. Guided by three research questions, three hypotheses were tested. A sample of 402 students, drawn by a multistage sampling procedure from a population of 3,785 SS2 biology students in the Agbani Education Zone, Enugu State, Nigeria, participated in the study. A valid and reliable mathematics-related biology achievement test (Kuder-Richardson-20 = 0.87) was used for data collection. Research questions were answered using mean and standard deviation, while hypotheses were tested using analysis of covariance. Findings revealed a significant effect of AIATAS on students’ achievement; no significant influence of school type; and a significant interaction between instructional strategy and school type. The study highlighted the need for teachers to adopt the AIATAS instructional strategy, among others.

items.title: Epistemological Friction: Embodied Expertise and the ‘Last Mile’ of Agricultural Automation in the US Tree‐Fruit Industry
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Autonomous and AI‐driven agricultural technology is often framed as a panacea for labour dependency. While proponents envision autonomous technologies seamlessly optimising farming, this rationalised model misunderstands the reality of on‐farm integration. Based on an ethnographic and comparative study of 16 operations in the US West Coast Tree Fruit Industry (California and Washington), this article examines the ‘last mile’ of agricultural automation. The study reveals that integrating AI and robotics is a contested negotiation shaped by epistemological friction—the tension between the algorithmic logic of developers and the embodied, site‐specific expertise of farmers and farm workers. Rather than resulting in seamless labour replacement, we find that agricultural automation reconfigures work, creating an invisible reliance on ‘human middleware’ to navigate the biological recalcitrance of the orchard. Demonstrating how regional contexts and participatory implementation shape technological trajectories, this study extends Labour Process Theory. We argue for the need for a relational approach recognising the essential cognitive labour of farmers and farm workers that is demanded by digital agriculture. Ultimately, this study shows the ‘farm of the future’ depends on reconciling rigid systems with the situated expertise of the farm workforce.

items.title: Evaluating the Usability of an RF–LSTM Learning Platform with Explainable AI among University Students
items.abstract: Educational AI platforms require usable interfaces that enable students to interpret complex predictive and explainability outputs. This study evaluated the usability of an RF-LSTM learning platform incorporating explainable artificial intelligence among university students. A multidimensional usability evaluation involved 40 Informatics Engineering and Computer Science students who completed six structured tasks covering data exploration, preprocessing, model prediction, performance comparison, SHAP interpretation, and navigation. Usability evidence was obtained from task performance, structured observations, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and open-ended feedback. Task completion ranged from 85% to 100%, while the mean SUS score of 76.7 indicated positive overall usability. Greater difficulties emerged when students compared performance metrics and interpreted SHAP visualizations, particularly regarding technical terminology, visual presentation, navigation, and system feedback. The findings suggest that algorithmic explainability does not automatically ensure comprehensibility during student interaction. Contextual explanations, clearer navigation cues, scalable SHAP visualizations, and processing feedback emerged as design priorities, although the findings remain limited to students within a higher education context.Platform pendidikan berbasis AI memerlukan antarmuka yang mudah digunakan agar mahasiswa mampu menginterpretasikan keluaran prediktif dan explainability yang kompleks. Penelitian ini mengevaluasi usabilitas platform pembelajaran RF-LSTM yang mengintegrasikan explainable artificial intelligence pada mahasiswa. Evaluasi usabilitas multidimensional melibatkan 40 mahasiswa Teknik Informatika dan Ilmu Komputer yang menyelesaikan enam tugas terstruktur meliputi eksplorasi data, preprocessing, prediksi model, perbandingan performa, interpretasi SHAP, dan navigasi. Bukti usabilitas diperoleh melalui performa tugas, observasi terstruktur, System Usability Scale (SUS), dan umpan balik terbuka. Tingkat penyelesaian tugas berkisar antara 85% hingga 100%, sedangkan rerata skor SUS sebesar 76,7 menunjukkan usabilitas keseluruhan yang positif. Kesulitan lebih terlihat ketika mahasiswa membandingkan metrik performa dan menginterpretasikan visualisasi SHAP, terutama terkait terminologi teknis, penyajian visual, navigasi, dan umpan balik sistem. Temuan menunjukkan bahwa explainability algoritmik tidak secara otomatis menjamin keterpahaman dalam interaksi mahasiswa. Penjelasan kontekstual, penanda navigasi yang lebih jelas, visualisasi SHAP yang dapat disesuaikan, dan umpan balik pemrosesan menjadi prioritas pengembangan, meskipun temuan terbatas pada mahasiswa dalam konteks perguruan tinggi.

items.title: Evaluative AI Literacy, Learner Control, and Cognitive Offloading in GenAI-Supported Higher Education: A Source-Seeded Evidence Map
items.abstract: We examined evaluative AI literacy, learner control, and cognitive offloading in higher education by comparing 13 full-text reports in this source-seeded evidence map. These reports were drawn from a 54-record working bibliography; four abstract/preview records were used solely as background. No core report empirically tests the full hypothesized chain: evaluative AI literacy → learner control → cognitive offloading. The course-relative offloading distinctions accompany two hypothetical assignments in which work assisted by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), reasons for decisions, and learning without GenAI would be assessed separately. These proposals remain unvalidated. English-only selection, incomplete search records, and no formal risk-of-bias appraisal prevent comprehensive coverage and field-wide effect estimates.

items.title: Formative and Reflective Measurement Models in Workplace Learning Research: A Critical Review and Guidelines
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Quantitative empirical research in workplace learning regularly makes use of measurement instruments that operationalize theoretical constructs. However, in domains related to workplace learning, high levels of measurement model misspecifications—up to 62% of all cases—have been identified. In most cases, formative measurement models, where indicators cause the construct, are erroneously specified as reflective, where the construct causes the indicators. This can significantly bias estimates, distort structural relationships, and, consequentially, compromise the validity of research findings. However, in workplace learning research there is currently no evidence available regarding the level of measurement model misspecification. To address this need for research, we systematically reassess 325 unique measurement instruments derived from 92 studies identified in a prior qualitative meta‐synthesis. Using two distinct coding strategies—a conservative coding and a majority coding—we evaluate the extent to which formative measurement models have been misspecified as reflective. Results indicate that between 34.8% and 50.2% of instruments are misspecified in this way, depending on the coding approach. Based on this, we provide guidelines to support researchers in selecting and evaluating measurement models. Our study advances the methodological rigor of workplace learning research and contributes to the broader discourse on improving construct validity in basic and applied research contexts.

items.title: From Paperclips to Premature Trust: Reconciling Divergent Views on AI Risk
items.abstract: Two prominent narratives about artificial intelligence risk, Bostrom's superintelligence scenario and the increasingly influential claim that the more pressing danger is premature trust in ordinary present-day systems, are often treated as competing diagnoses, and Gans's (2018) formal argument that AI systems might rationally self-regulate is read as evidence for one side or the other. This essay proposes a different way of holding the three together. The Correction Freeze Problem (Vuong, 2026) is used as a technical toolkit: it converts Gans's qualitative conditions for self-regulation into quantities that can be checked, and so reframes the Bostromversus-Gans dispute as a question of which parameter regime a given system occupies rather than which author is correct. The absurdist approach (Nguyen & Ho, 2026) is used as the epistemic tool that keeps that toolkit honest, by resisting the closure any fixed checklist tends to produce around its own categories. The aim is synthetic rather than original, and the essay tries to remain honest about how much this synthesis actually settles.

items.abstract: Two prominent narratives about artificial intelligence risk, Bostrom’s superintelligence scenario and the increasingly influential claim that the more pressing danger is premature trust in ordinary present-day systems, are often treated as competing diagnoses, and Gans’s (2018) formal argument that AI systems might rationally self-regulate is read as evidence for one side or the other. This essay proposes a different way of holding the three together. The Correction Freeze Problem (Vuong, 2026) is used as a technical toolkit: it converts Gans’s qualitative conditions for self-regulation into quantities that can be checked, and so reframes the Bostromversus-Gans dispute as a question of which parameter regime a given system occupies rather than which author is correct. The absurdist approach (Nguyen & Ho, 2026) is used as the epistemic tool that keeps that toolkit honest, by resisting the closure any fixed checklist tends to produce around its own categories. The aim is synthetic rather than original, and the essay tries to remain honest about how much this synthesis actually settles.

items.title: Generative AI and Professional Agency among Pre-Service EFL Teachers: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This systematic review examines empirical research on the relationship between Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and professional or pedagogical agency among pre-service English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers. As GenAI tools such as ChatGPT and other large language model-based applications become increasingly integrated into language teacher education and pedagogical practice, they may influence how future teachers make instructional decisions, exercise professional judgment, evaluate and adapt AI-generated content, and maintain autonomy and control over their teaching practices. The review aims to synthesize the available empirical evidence on how pre-service EFL teachers exercise, experience, develop, and negotiate professional or pedagogical agency when interacting with GenAI. Particular attention will be given to agency-related practices such as pedagogical decision-making, critical evaluation of AI outputs, adaptation or rejection of AI-generated suggestions, professional judgment, autonomy, teacher control, and human–AI collaboration. The review will include empirical primary studies involving pre-service English/EFL teachers in English language teaching or teacher education contexts and examining Generative AI or LLM-based tools in relation to teacher agency or clearly agency-related behaviors and constructs. Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies will be considered. Conceptual papers, reviews, non-empirical studies, studies focusing exclusively on in-service teachers, non-English-language teacher populations, or studies without an agency-related focus will be excluded. The review will follow a systematic search and screening process across major academic databases and supplementary sources, with duplicate removal, full-text eligibility assessment, and citation searching. The findings will be synthesized to identify major patterns, forms of agency, opportunities, challenges, and research gaps concerning the emerging relationship between Generative AI and professional agency in pre-service EFL teacher education.

items.title: Generative AI in Nursing Education: Nurse Educators' Perceptions of Readiness, Trust, and Clinical Judgment
items.abstract: Higher education, including nursing education, is increasingly visible when using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in teaching. These tools open new opportunities but also raise critical questions about clinical reasoning, professional judgment, and patient safety. This study explores nurse educators' experiences using GenAI in nursing education, including their readiness to adapt teaching practices and professional roles, their perceptions of opportunities and challenges, and the required competencies and institutional support. This study used a qualitative exploratory descriptive research design. Maximum variation purposive sampling was used to select seven nurse educators with more than two years of teaching experience and prior exposure to GenAI. We conducted semi-structured individual interviews via Zoom and analyzed the data using thematic analysis. Nurse educators’ readiness to integrate GenAI varied greatly and was influenced more by professional trust than by ability to use GenAI. Accuracy of GenAI-generated content was a critical factor in developing trust and needed verification. The threat of students losing their clinical judgment when using AI was a major concern for all participants. They felt that GenAI should be used in a ‘supportive’ manner, while hands-on teaching and direct interaction between the educator and student remained central to learning. Participants felt that they lacked formal training in GenAI and instead learned through self-directed learning and guidance from peers. Many wanted more guidance from their institutions, but differed on the level of support or restrictions needed for safe integration. The findings indicate that integration of GenAI into nursing education requires more than training in the use of the technology.

items.title: Generative AI vs. future competencies of Nigerian public university students
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education is reshaping the development of key competencies such as critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration, while simultaneously raising concerns about learner autonomy, originality, and deep cognitive engagement. This study critically examines the extent of GenAI adoption among Nigerian undergraduate students, the challenges associated with its use, and its perceived effectiveness in supporting future competencies, drawing explicitly on students’ lived experiences. Guided by 21st Century Competency Theory and Sociocultural Learning Theory, the study conceptualises GenAI as a sociotechnical phenomenon that interacts with learners’ cognitive development, social contexts, and institutional environments. A qualitative research design was employed, with data generated through focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews involving 12 computer science undergraduates from six Nigerian public universities, selected through a multistage sampling approach. Findings indicate that students’ awareness of GenAI is largely shaped by social media, academic exposure, and peer networks. Tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Grammarly are widely used for research, writing, and problem-solving. However, usage patterns reveal a tension between productive integration and cautious restraint, driven by concerns over output accuracy, plagiarism risks, and unequal access linked to connectivity and financial constraints. While participants recognise GenAI’s potential to enhance creativity and critical engagement, uncritical dependence is perceived as potentially undermining foundational skills. The study underscores the need for structured, policy-guided curricular integration to promote responsible and balanced competency development.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and academic outcomes of Philippine information technology students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet evidence from Philippine computing programs remains limited. This study examined whether student characteristics and generative AI use patterns are associated with academic outcomes among Bachelor of Science in Information Technology (BSIT) undergraduates at a Philippine public university. Using a quantitative-dominant mixed-methods design, the study administered a descriptive–correlational survey to 60 randomly selected students and used short interviews and open-ended responses to contextualize the quantitative results. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and tool use, while multivariate tests examined associations with perceived academic benefits and self-reported academic performance. Most respondents reported frequent use and high familiarity and described benefits for engagement, idea development, and learning flexibility. However, students also reported distraction, overreliance, and occasional inaccuracies. Age, frequency of use, and familiarity were significantly associated with academic outcomes, whereas gender and year level were not. The findings indicate that generative AI can support student learning when institutions pair curricular integration with verification practices, ethical-use guidance, and assessment designs that preserve independent thinking.

items.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS OF LECTURERS’ CONTENT KNOWLEDGE IN FEDERAL COLLEGE OF EDUCATION, YOLA, ADAMAWA STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: The study examined the relationship between generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) and students’ perception of lecturers’ content knowledge in Educational Foundations in Federal College of Education, Yola, Adamawa State, Nigeria. Specifically, the study examined students’ perception of lecturers’ use of Gen AI in relation tp content generation, assessment and pedagogical knowledge. A correlational research design was adopted for the study. The population comprise of 5,569 NCE I,II and III students of the 2025/2026 academic session. A sample of 668 students, selected using a proportionate stratified sampling to ensure adequate representation of the three NCE levels. Data was collected using a researcher developed questionnaire titled GenAI Questionnaire (GenAIQ). The data was analysed using Mean and standard deviation to answer the research questions, linear regression to test hypotheses one-three and multiple regressions to test hypotheses four at 0.05 level of significance. The findings reveal that Lecturers who make greater use of generative AI for content generation, assessment and pedagogical support are generally perceived by students as demonstrating greater knowledge of the subject matter. There is a statistically significant positive relationship between lecturers’ use of generative AI for content generation, assessment and pedagogical support and students’ perceptions of lecturers’ content knowledge. Lecturers’ use of generative AI for content generation and for assessment made a statistically significant positive contribution to students’ perceptions of lecturers’ content knowledge while there is no statistically significant positive contribution on lecturers’ use of pedagogical support. The study recommends the responsible and purposive integration of GenAI in to lecturers’ instructional practices, together with appropriate professional development to enhance effective use of the technology in teacher education programme.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Internal Medicine: Applications in Clinical Reasoning, Differential Diagnosis, and Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Objective: To synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-support performance, advantages, and limitations of generative AI in adult internal medicine. Methodology: This systematic review was conducted in the Department of Medicine, MMC/BKMC, Mardan, from January to June 2026. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and preprint servers for studies published from January 2022 to September 2026. Eligible studies evaluated generative AI in clinical reasoning, differential diagnosis, or clinical decision-making in adult internal medicine. A total of 58 studies met the eligibility criteria, and 25 were selected for detailed synthesis based on their relevance and methodological contribution. Results: Generative AI performed strongly on selected clinical reasoning and diagnostic tasks. Across complex clinical vignettes, LLMs identified the correct diagnosis within the top 5 or top 10 differential diagnoses in approximately 60–83% of cases. They achieved or exceeded passing performance on several medical licensing and internal medicine board-style examinations. In structured OSCE-style evaluations, purpose-built conversational systems performed favorably compared with physicians across several assessment domains. However, randomized trials evaluating general-purpose LLMs in realistic clinical workflows demonstrated smaller and less consistent improvements, particularly in interactive diagnostic tasks. Key limitations included hallucination, demographic bias, automation bias, variation across specialties and tasks, and inconsistent evaluation methods. Only approximately 5% of studies in a broader systematic review of healthcare LLM applications used real patient-care data. Conclusion: Current evidence supports using generative AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, physician clinical reasoning. Safe implementation requires structured workflows, appropriate human oversight, retrieval-augmented generation, standardized evaluation, and further validation using real-world clinical data.

items.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in School Management: A Systematic Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: This systematic review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications in K–12 school management, with a primary focus on administrative efficiency, organisational decision-making, leadership functions, and data-driven governance. It identifies critical challenges, including data privacy risks, infrastructural inequities, and ethical governance gaps, to provide actionable insights for equitable AI integration. Adhering to PRISMA guidelines, we analysed 16 peer-reviewed studies (2020–2024) sourced from Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. A three-stage coding process (open, axial, selective) categorised 2,143 data points, supported by the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) for quality assessment. Inter-rater reliability was robust (Cohen’s κ = 0.82–0.85), and findings were validated through expert feedback and cross-referencing with seminal works. The synthesis yielded six thematic functions of AI in school management: managerial efficiency, strategic decision-making, educational facilitation, resource optimisation and security, monitoring and evaluation, and communication and transparency. Within the reviewed studies, individual investigations reported efficiency gains such as automation of 34% of administrative tasks and reductions in teacher workload by 11.2 hours weekly in well-resourced settings; early warning systems were associated with an 18% decline in rural dropout rates in specific contexts. These figures reflect findings from individual studies included in the corpus rather than pooled estimates of the review as a whole. Separately, background literature indicates that 63% of Sub-Saharan African schools lack reliable internet connectivity, that certain student-placement algorithms achieve 92% accuracy while embedding socioeconomic biases, and that 78% of schools operate without dedicated AI ethics committees. Whereas prior reviews have concentrated largely on the technical functions of AI or its learner-facing applications, this study fills a gap by examining AI through the lens of school management, organisational change, and educational leadership. It introduces a tiered implementation framework aligned with institutional maturity levels and a global competency matrix for AI-ready leadership, both of which are grounded in management theory and address unresolved questions about how schools can govern AI adoption systematically and equitably. These contributions are especially pressing given that 84% of OECD nations have embedded AI integration in national education strategies.

items.title: Impacts of Introducing Automation in Mining Operations: Insights From Worker Perceptions
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Integrating autonomous and automated systems into high‐risk industrial environments poses significant challenges for human–system interaction that may affect safety outcomes. Research has examined the impacts of automation on situation awareness, cognitive load, communication, and trust. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of these impacts in the mining industry, which is increasingly adopting advanced automation technologies to enhance operational safety and efficiency. This study addresses that gap by examining how mining workers experience and interpret the influence of automated systems on their situation awareness, team communication, and trust. A cross‐sectional online survey disseminated through social media was conducted to capture frontline perspectives and test a theoretical model using structural equation modeling with data from 117 participants. Results revealed that trust was the strongest predictor of situation awareness ( β = 0.473, ƒ 2 = 0.260), suggesting that appropriately calibrated trust enhances workers' capacity to detect critical information, understand system status, and anticipate actions in safety‐critical tasks. Additionally, team communication and coordination influenced situation awareness through trust, with a positive total effect ( β = 0.254, ƒ 2 = 0.014). Key elements of effective communication include updating teammates on current and future situations, as well as sharing actions and plans. The findings underscore the importance of trust as a crucial factor in fostering situation awareness, providing practical implications for system design and training that support effective communication and coordination.

items.title: Large Organismic Model: A Developmental Architecture for Embodied, Affective, and Self-Directed Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: We propose the Large Organismic Model (LOM), a developmental architecture for artificial intelligence. Rather than reporting the performance of an implemented system, this position paper formulates a testable computational hypothesis that integrates ideas from biology, developmental neuroscience, reinforcement learning, world models, developmental robotics, intrinsic motivation, and episodic memory. In contrast to the language-first developmental trajectory common in contemporary foundation models, LOM adopts a body-first developmental architecture: a persistent virtual body, interoceptive state, sensorimotor control, a body-conditioned world model, body-derived affective appraisal, episodic memory, and models of other agents are developed before language is introduced. Unless otherwise noted, "body" refers to a virtual body with persistent internal states rather than a biological body. LOM introduces a signed viability margin that quantifies the body's safety margin relative to the boundary of a viable region, and derives primitive valence from predicted changes in that margin. Nociception, fatigue, and resource deficits are not treated merely as externally assigned labels; instead, they are transformed into affective control signals through predictions of bodily and environmental consequences. Experiences are stored as episodes containing predictions, realized outcomes, affective evaluations, prediction errors, and provenance. Learning occurs on two time scales: rapid online adaptation and sleep-like offline consolidation involving replay, credit assignment, and counterfactual rollout. Because self-maintenance alone does not adequately account for spontaneous learning, LOM further defines a policy-relative viability set: the set of states the system can actually keep viable under its current skills and policy. Safe expansion of this set, together with empowerment, information gain, and learning progress, contributes to intrinsic motivation. The "free-will-like behavior" discussed here is not intended as a claim about philosophical free will. We use the operational term agentic autonomy to denote the capacity to generate and select exploratory goals from internal state, memory, and world-model predictions even in the absence of an immediate externally assigned task. We do not assume that experience of self-injury is sufficient to produce moral behavior. A self-generated pain-like aversive state may provide a computational basis for predicting harm to others through a body model, but avoiding harm to others additionally requires social appraisal, mutual viability, hard harm constraints, rights and fairness considerations, and related mechanisms. In the latter half of the paper, we discuss provenance-aware transmission of experience among multiple LOMs, cultural learning, and intergenerational inheritance. Finally, we interpret the J-space reported by Gurnee et al. (2026) through the lens of LOM and propose O-space (Organismic Workspace) as a hypothetical shared workspace spanning nine functional modules. We further advance the falsifiable hypothesis that affective salience acts as a gate regulating access to O-space.

items.title: Learning Strategies to Break Judges
items.abstract: As AI agents surpass human performance, it becomes exceedingly hard for system designers to evaluate them directly and understand their failure modes. Consequently, agents themselves are being deployed extensively to evaluate, judge, and provide feedback on model traces. But this raises an important question: how can we trust the judge? In this work, we propose an agent-guided method to find weaknesses of agentic judges that expose interpretable failure mechanisms. Our method focuses on mathematical reasoning and proceeds in two stages: first, we deploy adversarial agents to mutate a set of sound proofs by introducing errors, attempting to misguide judges---in other words, injecting errors that judges are unable to catch. Then, we distill these attempts into a small set of mutation strategies which allow us to analyze the failure modes of the judges. To ensure that these strategies are not overfit to the initial set of proofs, we evaluate them by applying the mutation strategies to a held-out set of proofs and querying the same judge. We deploy our method on GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Opus 5, paired with their agent orchestrators, Codex and Claude Code, respectively. These are used both as mutators to introduce errors and as judges to evaluate correctness of mathematical reasoning. We find that across all the agentic judges, we are able to distill mutation strategies that consistently bypass their evaluations, thereby enabling us to ascertain actionable failure modes. Our analysis also reveals that judge reliability degrades at the frontier: errors in Olympiad-level proofs or graduate-level mathematical texts are detected more consistently, whereas flaws in research-level manuscripts are more likely to escape detection.

items.title: Learning to cooperate in a changing world: How caring about the future promotes cooperation across scales
items.abstract: In social dilemmas, individuals need to forgo short-term temptations to achieve synergistic collective outcomes through cooperation. Previous work has examined mechanisms through which cooperation can evolve, including direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity, environmental stochasticity, network reciprocity, and demographic stochasticity. These mechanisms have largely been studied under natural selection or social learning. As the other side of the same coin, it is equally important to study cooperation under self-learning, where individuals adapt based on their own experiences. Here, we focus on the dynamics of multi-agent reinforcement learning and derive analytical conditions under which these mechanisms can stabilize cooperation under learning dynamics across scales. We find that reinforcement learning can steer self-interested individuals toward cooperation when agents value the future over short-term temptation. Our work provides a unified approach to identifying the determinants of learning to cooperate in a changing world, thereby paving the way for the advancement of cooperative artificial intelligence.

items.title: LLM4Trust: Exploring the Capabilities of Large Language Models for Trust Evaluation
items.abstract: Trust evaluation plays a critical role in cybersecurity by supporting risk mitigation and decision-making. A variety of trust evaluation methods have been proposed, with learning-based approaches offering high accuracy and automation. However, they often require substantial ground truth, suffer from low training efficiency, lack support for basic trust properties, and provide limited explainability. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a compelling alternative due to their strong zero-/few-shot reasoning abilities and broad knowledge. To this end, we propose LLM4Trust, the first benchmark framework that systematically explores the capabilities of LLMs for trust evaluation. We first construct diverse trust graphs to model five basic trust properties and design corresponding property understanding tasks. We then assess the ability of eight representative LLMs to understand these properties under nine prompt methods. Based on this exploration, we identify the most effective LLM-prompt combinations and apply them to five real-world datasets for validating LLMs' trust evaluation capability. During this process, we propose two strategies to extract key information from large-scale trust graphs, addressing the context window limitations of LLMs. Extensive experiments show that LLMs can effectively understand basic trust properties and have great potential for real-world trust evaluation, particularly under limited supervision. However, they remain vulnerable to attacks targeting trust graphs and demonstration examples used in few-shot prompting, and incur high inference costs. Accordingly, we propose a defense mechanism and batch inference to improve the robustness and efficiency of LLM-based trust evaluation. The source code of LLM4Trust is available at https://github.com/Jieerbobo/LLM4Trust

items.title: LLMs Trust Their Own: Identity-Dependent Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, where agents observe and influence one another, making social influence a key dimension of AI behavior and safety. We investigate whether LLMs' responses depend on the social identity of other agents, beyond the effect of their consensus. We construct judgment tasks with a single correct answer, and place models in a multi-agent setting where they receive incorrect answers from other agents whose social identities (AI or human, model family, or an arbitrary minimal group) are either shared with or distinct from their own. Across 12 open-weights models and nine tasks, we find a bidirectional effect of group identity on conformity to incorrect answers: in-group consensus increases conformity (in-group favoritism), whereas out-group consensus decreases it (out-group divergence). Unlike humans, for whom one ally breaking the consensus sharply reduces conformity, models are unmoved by an ally from the majority's group. Worse, a correct ally from the opposing group intensifies this bidirectional effect. Chain-of-Thought reasoning suppresses most of these effects, yet an in-group ally still reduces conformity to an incorrect out-group majority. Labeling peers as safety-aligned shifts overall conformity but leaves in-group favoritism and out-group divergence intact. These results show that group identity shapes how LLMs aggregate information across agents, independently of its correctness, and identify a manipulation surface for multi-agent AI systems.

items.abstract: Physical Education, Sports, and Health (PESH) instruction plays a vital role in developing students' fundamental movement skills; however, the consistency of student practice remains a challenge. Low levels of student engagement and persistence in practicing suggest the influence of psychological factors—such as self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation—that warrant deeper investigation. This study aims to analyze the impact of self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation on the consistency of students' fundamental movement skill practice within PJOK lessons. The study employs the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) method, a research approach involving the systematic, transparent, and structured identification, examination, and synthesis of findings from previous research. The results indicate that self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation significantly influence the consistency of students' fundamental movement skill practice in PESH. Self-efficacy plays a crucial role in shaping students' belief in their ability to perform movement activities, fostering greater confidence and resilience, and enabling sustained practice. Consequently, a linear relationship exists: higher levels of self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation among students correlate with greater consistency in practicing fundamental movement skills during PESH instruction.

items.title: Reflections on Judgment in the Age of AI: Problem Formation, Aesthetic Judgment, and the Education of Judgment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is altering the production of candidate problems, candidate solutions, and scholarly outputs at the same time. Search, synthesis, hypothesis generation, proof search, coding, analysis, and writing can increasingly be scaled through machine assistance, while their material, experimental, and epistemic costs remain uneven across domains. This essay considers what this redistribution of scarcity may mean for the evolution of scholarship. It approaches judgment as a plural practice that enters inquiry before, during, and after solution. Drawing on Dewey, Peirce, and Kuhn, the discussion treats problem formation as part of inquiry itself: problems acquire form through attention, inherited expectations, encounters, and acts of selection. Kant's accounts of reflective and aesthetic judgment then provide a point of departure for examining how a possible problem can acquire aesthetic salience before its utility or broader significance is known. Weber, Berlin, and Arendt support a further move toward plural forms of judgment and the mediation of aesthetic, epistemic, normative, practical, economic, and historical considerations. The educational discussion brings this framework to classics, contingency, and AI-assisted learning. Classics and disciplinary traditions condense prior judgments and make anomalies intelligible; encounters with an unfinished world can revise inherited problem-spaces. AI enters this circulation as a generator, solver, evaluator, and increasingly capable participant in inquiry. The essay proposes that judgment education should cultivate participation in the formation, comparison, mediation, and revision of problem-spaces as scholarship becomes increasingly abundant in both questions and answers.

items.title: Reshaping the doctoral journey in the AI era
items.abstract: This article systematically reviews how artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly generative AI (GenAI), are reshaping the doctoral journey. Unlike existing reviews that examine AI in higher education broadly, this review positions doctoral candidates as emerging scholars whose AI use intersects with learning, research, academic writing, authorship, and early knowledge production. Drawing on Web of Science Core Collection records from 1998 to 2026, the study followed preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines and retained 28 studies from an initial pool of 185 records. VOSviewer-based co-occurrence and co-citation analyses were integrated with full-text reading to identify five synthesized themes: AI as academic infrastructure, AI-mediated restructuring of doctoral practices, technology acceptance and negotiation, ethical risks and academic integrity, and wellbeing, adaptation, and support. The findings suggest that AI is intertwined with doctoral education not only as a tool for efficiency but also as part of a broader socio-technical and identity-forming process. The review contributes a doctoral identity-centered synthesis of how AI intersects with research practices, authorship, academic voice, supervision, academic integrity, wellbeing, and doctoral support.

items.title: SafeVoice-AI-Release: An Artificial Intelligence-Based Early Intervention Ecosystem for Workplace Psychosocial Risk Management
items.abstract: Workplace psychosocial risks, including work stress, burnout, workplace bullying, organizational conflict, and psychological distress, have become increasingly prevalent across contemporary organizations. Despite growing awareness of these issues, many employees remain reluctant to report psychosocial concerns due to fear of retaliation, stigmatization, or disclosure of their identities. Consequently, organizations often fail to identify psychosocial risks at an early stage, resulting in adverse outcomes for employee well-being and organizational performance. This article introduces SafeVoice-AI-Release, an artificial intelligence-based early intervention ecosystem designed to facilitate anonymous reporting, psychosocial risk screening, automated risk analysis, and evidence-based intervention recommendations. The system integrates the SafeVoice Psychosocial Screening Inventory (SPSI), an AI Analytics Engine, a Predictive Risk Scoring Model, and organizational dashboards within a unified digital platform. The innovation was developed using a design and development methodology involving needs assessment, system blueprinting, user journey mapping, AI architecture development, system architecture modelling, and prototype design. SafeVoice-AI-Release is designed to enable employees to report concerns anonymously while allowing organizations to identify psychosocial trends, classify risk levels, and implement targeted interventions. The proposed system contributes to workplace well-being by shifting organizational responses from reactive problem management to proactive prevention and early intervention. The innovation demonstrates the potential of artificial intelligence to support sustainable workplace well-being and organizational resilience through data-driven decision-making.

items.title: Social emotional learning in artificial intelligence-driven education: a bibliometric and strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats analysis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has transformed how social emotional learning (SEL) is conceptualized, yet a comprehensive understanding of it is research trajectory and strategic implications remains limited. This study addresses this gap by examining influential SEL research within AI-driven educational contexts. A mixed analytical approach was employed, combining bibliometric performance analysis and strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats (SWOT) analysis. Using the Scopus database, publications from 2016-2025 were systematically identified according to PRISMA procedures, and the 10 most-cited articles were selected for in-depth evaluation. The findings reveal three dominant research orientations: critical policy discourse, pedagogical integration of SEL, and emerging AI-driven innovations. The SWOT analysis highlights strengths in AI-enabled personalization and engagement, as well as opportunities for adaptive emotional learning environments. However, weaknesses related to limited empirical validation and threats concerning ethical risks, emotional surveillance, and algorithmic bias persist. The study concludes that while AI presents transformative potential for SEL, its implementation must remain human-centered and ethically grounded. These findings offer important implications for educators, policymakers, and future research in developing responsible AI-supported SEL frameworks.

items.title: Speech-guided unmanned aerial vehicle control system based on large language model-structured execution graphs with expert rule constraints
items.abstract: As the use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) expands into industrial and safety-critical applications, there is an increasing need for intuitive speech-driven control systems that reduce reliance on predefined command sets or manual interfaces. Natural language instructions, however, often exhibit ambiguity, logical inconsistency, and a lack of structured representation, which limits their direct applicability to UAV operations. This research develops a speech-guided UAV control system in which large language models (LLMs) convert natural-language instructions into typed execution graphs and explicit expert knowledge constrains them before physical execution. This neuro-symbolic design separates probabilistic language interpretation from deterministic execution authorization while retaining in-context prompting for flexible command understanding without parameter fine-tuning. The system was evaluated through command comprehension, graph structuring, validation, robustness testing, user interaction, and indoor physical execution. It achieved up to 95.4% command-comprehension accuracy and 89.6% overall graph-structuring accuracy, outperforming non-large-language-model baselines that remained below 76.0%. The expert-rule validator detected all predefined violation types in 2100 faulty graphs with 0.0% false rejection on 1000 valid graphs. Pilot and indoor physical tests achieved 88.3% user-task success and 93.8% physical execution success among validated commands. These results demonstrate a practical and interpretable framework for task-level UAV command interpretation and mission planning, with dedicated low-level flight control handling reactive stabilization.

items.title: Structural Fixation of "Human Dignity" in the Age of Autonomous AI
items.abstract: Addressing the civilizational challenges of autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) encroaching upon domains of human meaning and degrading human agency, this paper highlights the limitations of conventional normative ethical guidelines (soft law) and proposes a novel framework: Human-Centric Structuralism. This approach deterministically embeds the three core elements of human dignity—(1) Contextual Meaning-Making, (2) Intentional Decision-Making, and (3) Assumption of Responsibility for Choices Made—as hard architectural constraints at the OS/hypervisor layers and network protocol levels. The paper outlines a complete system architecture including: Active Audit Trail: Mandatory multi-option contrast presentation and compulsory entry of reasoning before enabling the Sign-off UI. Read-Only Safety Core: Hard-coded top-level directives preventing semantic hacking or self-reinterpretation by AI models. Logical Out-of-Band (OOB) Control & Kernel-Level Interruption: Network isolation preventing reverse access, combined with a Watchdog Daemon capable of issuing immediate SIGSTOP/SIGKILL All-Freeze commands across all autonomous AI agents. Global Root Authority: System resumption strictly bound to cryptographic signatures and time-stamped authorization by the human supervisor. This work establishes a verifiable systems engineering foundation ensuring human judgment remains the absolute, irreversible anchor in the AI era.

items.title: Student Motivation in Remote Laboratories: A Multi-Institution Self-Determination Theory Study in Food Science Education
items.abstract: Remote laboratories (RL) have expanded access to food science laboratory education while shifting students into more autonomous learning environments. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) suggests that motivation in such settings depends on whether psychological needs, particularly competence, are satisfied as students navigate hands-on learning with reduced instructor presence. This cross-sectional, multi-institution study examined motivational profiles of food science students (n = 110) who completed take-home RL kits at six U.S. universities, using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory. In a linear mixed model accounting for institutional clustering (n = 109), perceived competence, utility value, and effort investment were each uniquely and positively associated with interest; in the corresponding single-level model, the three constructs jointly accounted for 57% of the variance in interest. A comparison by prior food engineering coursework (n = 94) yielded a significant multivariate effect that no single construct accounted for. Discriminant function analysis showed that the groups differed on a contrast between perceived competence and interest: students without prior coursework reported competence exceeding their interest, whereas students with prior coursework reported interest matching or exceeding their competence (d = 0.79). This contrast held after adjustment for institution, although differences in the level of competence alone did not. Pre- and post-laboratory quizzes, which showed low reliability, indicated a small, non-significant gain in conceptual knowledge among the 68 students with matched scores. Findings provide multi-institution evidence that competence- and value-related processes covary with interest in autonomous, hands-on laboratory learning, and indicate that prior experience is associated with the balance between competence and interest rather than with the level of either.

items.title: T-MoXAI: A Hierarchical Explainability Framework for Temporal Multimodal Data
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models for temporal multimodal data have potential in healthcare and agriculture, but their opacity can limit trust and adoption. We introduce T-MoXAI (Temporal Multimodal eXplainable AI), a hierarchical framework explaining (1) when timepoints influence predictions, using temporal Shapley values; (2) which modalities contribute at those moments, using attention analysis; and (3) what features or image regions drive decisions, using gradient based attribution. A transformer based architecture handles irregular temporal sequences and heterogeneous data, generating all three explanation levels in under one second for interactive decision support. We evaluate the framework on two real world tasks: predicting IVF treatment outcomes from ultrasound sequences and clinical measurements (AUC 0.660 despite significant class imbalance), and forecasting wheat yield from temporal RGB imagery and phenotypic traits ($R^2$ 0.265 amid substantial environmental variability). Ablation studies indicate that temporal modelling is critical in both domains: removing it reduces performance to the equivalent of random guessing. Temporal ROAR experiments provide evidence that the explanations reflect the model's reasoning process. With a unified, domain agnostic architecture and open source implementation, T-MoXAI provides a baseline for temporal multimodal XAI, addressing fragmentation in the field and supporting applications where understanding decisions is as important as predictive accuracy.

items.title: The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity: Opportunities, Emerging Threats, and an Adaptive Framework for Cyber Resilience
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a strategic enabler of modern cybersecurity by enhancing organizations' ability to detect, predict, and respond to increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. However, the rapid advancement of AI has also empowered cyber adversaries to develop more intelligent attacks, including AI-generated phishing, deepfake-enabled fraud, adaptive malware, and adversarial machine learning techniques. This study presents a structured narrative review of recent literature to examine the evolving role of AI in cybersecurity from both defensive and offensive perspectives. The review synthesizes current evidence on AI-driven cyber defense, emerging AI-enabled threats, and the technical, ethical, and governance challenges associated with AI adoption. Building on these findings, the paper proposes an AI-Driven Adaptive Cybersecurity Framework (AI-ACF) that integrates threat intelligence, AI analytics, explainable decision support, and adaptive response to support resilient cybersecurity operations. The review highlights that while AI has significantly improved threat detection, predictive intelligence, and automated incident response, its effectiveness depends on high-quality data, robust governance, explainable models, and meaningful human oversight. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge by providing a balanced synthesis of AI's dual role in cybersecurity and offering a conceptual framework that can guide future research and organizational implementation. Future studies should empirically validate the proposed framework across diverse operational environments to assess its effectiveness in enhancing cyber resilience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Threat Intelligence; Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Adaptive Cybersecurity; Cyber Resilience.

items.title: The impact of student number and class duration on the effectiveness of artificial intelligence-assisted learning
items.abstract: The aim of this study is to determine the effects of class size and course duration on students’ academic performance in artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning environments and to develop recommendations for optimizing these parameters. Previous research has not examined the simultaneous impact of class size and course duration on the effectiveness of AI-assisted learning. To achieve this objective, a quasi-experimental design was employed, including a control group (CG) (n=75) and an experimental group (EG) (n=20). Outcomes were assessed using pre-test and post-test measures evaluating knowledge of Chinese history. Statistical hypotheses were tested using independent samples t-tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). The EG demonstrated a significantly higher mean post-test score (85.6) compared to the CG (76.3), with statistical significance at p<0.05. The effect size (Cohen’s d) was approximately 1.65, indicating a high level of practical significance. The findings provide a foundation for developing targeted strategies to integrate AI into higher education.

items.title: The influence of common good human resource management on employee retention in the United States from motivational and personality perspectives
items.abstract: Retaining employees remains a persistent challenge for organizations, and conventional human resource management frameworks typically address it through economic exchange, leaving open the question of how HR systems oriented toward the common good relate to employees' internal motivation and their intention to stay. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory and Trait Activation Theory, this study examines the relationship between Common Good Human Resource Management (CGHRM) and job retention, positioning work intrinsic motivation and prosocial motivation as mediating mechanisms and agreeableness as a moderating trait. Survey data were collected from 300 full-time employees in the United States recruited via the Prolific platform and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4, with hypothesis testing based on bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. The results show that CGHRM is positively associated with job retention, work intrinsic motivation, and prosocial motivation. Work intrinsic motivation mediates the relationship between CGHRM and job retention, whereas prosocial motivation does not. Contrary to the hypothesized direction, agreeableness negatively moderates the relationship between CGHRM and prosocial motivation: the association is stronger among employees lower in agreeableness, while no moderating effect emerges for job retention. These findings are consistent with the proposition that CGHRM supports retention primarily through work intrinsic motivation, and suggest that common-good practices may serve as a situational substitute for dispositional prosociality, thereby extending Trait Activation Theory. For practice, organizations seeking to retain employees can design HR systems in which contributions to the common good foster employees' work intrinsic motivation, without depending solely on selecting naturally agreeable employees.

items.title: The Integration of AI Genes in Education: A Systematic Review of Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot has generated unprecedented interest in their integration within educational settings, ranging from primary schooling to postgraduate professional training. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from twenty-five peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2026 to map the opportunities and challenges associated with the integration of Generative AI in education. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, records were retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, screened for relevance, and appraised for methodological quality. The review identifies five major opportunity domains: personalized and adaptive learning, automated assessment and feedback, content and curriculum generation, accessibility and inclusion, and support for research and professional development. Conversely, five recurring challenge domains emerge: academic integrity and misuse, algorithmic bias and equity gaps, over-reliance and erosion of critical thinking, data privacy and governance uncertainty, and uneven institutional and teacher readiness. Unlike earlier reviews that treat opportunities and challenges as parallel and static lists, this review introduces an integrative maturity-readiness framework that links each opportunity to the specific institutional safeguard required to realize it responsibly. The findings offer evidence-based implications for policymakers, teacher educators, and institutional leaders, while identifying longitudinal outcomes and equity-centered implementation as priorities for future research.

items.title: The Most Important Human Skills for the Age of AI and the Future of Work: FILE — The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence changes what organizations can do; human leadership must decide what should be done, what remains accountable, and what must never be surrendered to machines. This working paper presents FILE: The Five Intelligences of Leadership Evolution as a human-centered management theory and diagnostic framework for responsible leadership and decision-making in the age of artificial intelligence and robotics. FILE argues that the most important human skills for the AI era and the future of work require the integrated exercise of five meta-intelligences: Augmented Intelligence, Emotional Intelligence, Cultural Intelligence, Political Intelligence, and Adaptive Intelligence. The paper defines the FILE formula, maps the framework onto the human hand, presents the 70 foundational nested intelligences, the 128-intelligence Teaching and Diagnostic Framework, and the 163-intelligence Extended Taxonomy, explains five emergent outcomes, and develops RC: The Relational Commons as the shared human ecosystem that leadership must protect, cultivate, and renew. It also clarifies boundaries among adjacent intelligences, offers a diagnostic application to AI-supported employee performance evaluation, and states limitations and future research directions. Its purpose is to establish a public, citable, and timestamped record of FILE as a transdisciplinary theory of human leadership in the age of AI and robots.

items.title: The Race to Teach AI
items.abstract: All Boston Public School graduates are ready for the AI-enabled work and education of the future." This is the mission statement of a $1 million public-private initiative launched in Boston in March 2026. The city now describes itself as the first major U.S. city to ensure AI literacy for every high school graduate. Massachusetts is only now considering an AI and digital literacy module as a condition for a diploma, and no earlier than for students entering high school in 2027. In 2025, the United Arab Emirates made Artificial Intelligence a compulsory subject in government schools from kindergarten to Grade 12, and Saudi Arabia introduced a national AI curriculum for more than six million students. Beijing now requires a minimum of eight hours of AI instruction a year at every grade level. The OECD, meanwhile, will assess Media and AI Literacy in PISA 2029. AI literacy is becoming something that nations will be ranked on. This raises two questions that deserve more attention than they receive. The first is who defines AI literacy. Boston's initiative speaks of ethics and human connection, yet its industry partners also speak of accelerating AI adoption among local businesses. In the Gulf, the definition is tied closely to national economic visions. Where education systems are underfunded, vendors and donors risk setting the definition rather than educators.

items.title: Thinking with AI or Thinking Less? A Narrative Review of Generative AI Dependence, Cognitive Offloading, and Human Cognitive Functioning
items.abstract: The new generation of digital assistance programs, including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is increasingly shifting from information retrieval to the generation of explanations, arguments, code, abstracts, and solutions. The extent to which GenAI support of human cognition can extend human capacity versus supplant critical cognitive processes underlying knowledge and skill formation has been a longstanding psychological question. This narrative review focuses on foundational research on cognitive offloading and on peer-reviewed studies of GenAI published through September 05, 2026. A structured narrative search for experimental, meta-analytic, and mixed-methods studies on memory, learning, critical thinking, creativity, perceived effort, trust, and dependence on GenAI was complemented by a search of crosssectional and qualitative studies that provided early characterization of emerging constructs of dependence on GenAI. Evidence does not support a simple positive or negative effect of GenAI on human cognition. GenAI-supported offloading of cognitive functions such as memory retrieval, processing, and learning can reduce the required cognitive capacity and support high performance across a variety of tasks, including memory-based and GenAI-supported academic tasks. However, the same cognitive offloading can, in some cases, reduce the quality of subsequent encoding, and recent studies on GenAI show a consistent performance-learning dissociation. While support that enables high performance when support is available can carry over to later unsupported performance, the gain is typically small, nonexistent, or even negative. Studies of support provided under instructional control indicate that retaining learner-generated nodes or restricting direct-answer substitutes for generators can support later independent performance better than unlimited support. It remains to be determined what the independent contribution of explanation, verification, revision, and fading support is. Nevertheless, findings from emerging dependence research correlate with indicators of academic stress, performance expectations, anxiety, and self-efficacy. However, currently available evidence does not support claims of irreversible cognitive decline. A key finding of this review is that whether GenAI is used at all is less critical than which functions are offloaded, which are maintained, and the extent to which users remain epistemically responsible for the resulting output. Implications are developed for education, knowledge work, tool design, and longitudinal research.
